chapter: Handy, Bix and disputes over credit
title: Bix's repertoire and the Bob Crosby band copying his tunes
summary: He says musicians rehashed Dixieland numbers and the Bob Crosby band copied Fidgety Feet and Maryland, with Feist profiting.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: But also, I'd like to ask you, what are some of the tunes Bix recorded that you remember?

Well, he made Tomlin, blues, many of the Dixieland numbers. Then he did like the rest of them did. Took another tune, rehashed the Dixieland number, and he called it his own. Yeah. All musicians began to get the idea. And the closest that I had seen came to it was the Bob Crosby bunch. They take my fidgeted feet and they called it South Rampart Street Parade. Now, I bet you could play both of them together with only exception in the first part and the last part, the march, the break, the march part, the pudding, because I played . And they played the counter melody to that. And if you listen to them records, you know it, they style it too. Now, they were the only ones that I know that was getting close to what I used to do in a big scale. They took this Maryland, but there was nuts, because that had no part of Maryland. Maryland should have been with its own harmony, but they added a tune to themself that Leo Feist made money on it, and they got nothing. You understand what I mean? I don't know who created that part, but that's a different tune.
What did they call it? They called it Maryland.
They were staples that. You understand the story? My Maryland, my Maryland. Yes, I see. Then the cland of that would go .
Correct. Maryland. He did. A new arrangement on Maryland. They got exactly nothing. Anyone. Listen. If you take the time around. . . .
